title: Design & Innovation for Digital Business Transformation - Quiz DI1
subtitle: Multiple-choice questions based on Class 1 content (Slides 20–End) and student notes.

questions.question: According to the Technology Adoption Lifecycle, which group represents the smallest segment of adopters?
options: Early Majority
Late Majority
Innovators
Early Adopters
questions.explanation: Innovators represent only about 2.5% of the market, making them the smallest segment in the adoption lifecycle.

questions.question: The Technology S-Curve describes which of the following phenomena?
options: The linear growth of a technology's market share over time
The pattern of slow initial growth, rapid acceleration, and eventual maturity of a technology
The decline of old technologies as new ones emerge
The relationship between R&D investment and product revenue
questions.explanation: The S-Curve captures three phases: slow initial adoption, rapid growth, and plateau at maturity.

questions.question: Clayton Christensen's S-Curve framework distinguishes between two types of technologies. Which pair correctly identifies them?
options: Disruptive technologies and sustaining technologies
Component technologies and architectural technologies
General-purpose technologies and specialized technologies
Incremental technologies and radical technologies
questions.explanation: Christensen's S-Curve framework distinguishes between component technologies and architectural technologies.

questions.question: In Geoffrey Moore's Market Development Lifecycle, what is "The Chasm"?
options: The period of rapid growth when a technology reaches mainstream adoption
The gap between technology enthusiasts/visionaries and the pragmatic mainstream market
The decline phase when a technology becomes obsolete
The moment when a dominant design emerges in the market
questions.explanation: The Chasm is the critical gap between early market adopters and the pragmatic mainstream.

questions.question: According to the course framework, which phase comes AFTER "The Chasm" in Geoffrey Moore's model?
options: Early Market
Maturity
Bowling Alley and Tornado
Decline
questions.explanation: After crossing the Chasm, technologies enter the Bowling Alley and then the Tornado.

questions.question: A technology is described as being in the "Uncertainty Zone" in the course's adoption framework. What does this most likely correspond to?
options: The technology has reached full market saturation
The technology is in the Chasm — it has early adopters but has not yet proven mainstream viability
The technology is declining due to a superior replacement
The technology is in the innovators phase with no commercial application yet
questions.explanation: The Uncertainty Zone maps to the Chasm — a critical period where mainstream adoption is uncertain.

questions.question: What does a "Dominant Design" mean in the context of technology adoption?
options: The technology with the highest R&D investment in a given market
The product design that wins marketplace allegiance and becomes the standard competitors must follow
The technology adopted exclusively by large enterprises
The first technology to enter a new market
questions.explanation: A dominant design is the one that wins the allegiance of the marketplace.

questions.question: Which of the following is the best example of a "dominant design" transition in the audio industry?
options: From vinyl LP records to audio cassettes to CDs to streaming
From AM radio to FM radio to digital radio
From mono sound to stereo sound to surround sound
From physical music stores to online music stores
questions.explanation: LP → cassette → CD → streaming perfectly illustrates successive dominant designs in home audio.

questions.question: According to the student notes, where is Generative AI (e.g., ChatGPT, Copilot) positioned in the Technology Adoption Lifecycle?
options: Early Adopters
Early Majority
Late Majority
Laggards
questions.explanation: Generative AI tools like ChatGPT and Microsoft Copilot are in the Late Majority phase.

questions.question: According to the student notes, what is the PRIMARY bottleneck preventing Agentic AI from moving from Early Majority to Late Majority?
options: Lack of computational power
High cost of hardware infrastructure
Reliability, security, observability, and lack of human control
Absence of large language model capabilities
questions.explanation: The main barriers are reliability, security, observability, and lack of control.

questions.question: What does Moore's Law (1975 revision) state?
options: The number of internet users doubles every 18 months
The number of transistors in a microprocessor doubles every 2 years
The value of a network is proportional to the square of its users
The cost of computing halves every 5 years
questions.explanation: Moore revised his law to state that transistor count doubles approximately every 2 years.

questions.question: Which of the following is a direct consequence of Moore's Law?
options: The rise of social networks
Miniaturization of computing devices and the emergence of cyber-physical systems
The convergence of television, radio, and telecommunications
The growth of the attention economy
questions.explanation: Moore's Law enables miniaturization, embedded processors, sensors, and cyber-physical systems.

questions.question: Metcalfe's Law states that the value of a network is:
options: Equal to the number of its users
Proportional to the square of the number of its users
Inversely proportional to the number of competing networks
Determined by the quality of its infrastructure
questions.explanation: Metcalfe's Law states that network value is proportional to n², where n is the number of users.

questions.question: Reed's Law extends Metcalfe's Law by emphasizing which additional dimension of network value?
options: The speed of data transmission within the network
The importance of subgroups and communities within a network
The geographic reach of a network
The revenue generated per user
questions.explanation: Reed's Law highlights the value created by subgroups and communities within a network.

questions.question: Claude Shannon's Information Theory has which of the following key implications for the digital economy?
options: It proves that all information can be transmitted without loss
It establishes the relationship between data and information, and the capacity of media to handle signals
It defines the economic value of data as equivalent to oil
It explains why attention is a scarce resource in the digital age
questions.explanation: Shannon's theory formalizes the relationship between signals, bits of information, and channel capacity.

questions.question: According to Russel Ackoff (1967), what happens beyond a certain threshold of data?
options: The amount of information increases proportionally
The amount of information diminishes
The value of data becomes infinite
Data transforms automatically into knowledge
questions.explanation: Ackoff stated that beyond a certain amount of data, the amount of information actually diminishes.

questions.question: According to Bresnahan & Trajtenberg (1992), which THREE characteristics define a General Purpose Technology (GPT)?
options: Affordability, scalability, and network effects
Pervasiveness, inherent potential for technical improvements, and innovational complementarities
Disruption, speed of adoption, and market dominance
Open-source nature, global reach, and government support
questions.explanation: The three defining GPT characteristics are pervasiveness, inherent potential for improvements, and innovational complementarities.
questions.category: General Purpose Technologies & Long Innovation Cycles

questions.question: Which of the following is identified in the course as the most important General Purpose Technology of our era?
options: The Internet
Blockchain
Artificial Intelligence (particularly Machine Learning)
The Smartphone
questions.explanation: The course cites AI, particularly machine learning, as the most important GPT of our era.
questions.category: General Purpose Technologies & Long Innovation Cycles

questions.question: The concept of "long innovation cycles" (Kondratiev waves / Schumpeter) suggests that:
options: Technology adoption always takes more than 100 years
Each major economic cycle (50–60 years) is driven by a distinct technological innovation that permeates the entire economy
Innovation slows down as economies mature
Only government-funded research produces economy-wide technological change
questions.explanation: Each major economic cycle lasts about 50–60 years and is driven by a distinct cluster of innovations.
questions.category: General Purpose Technologies & Long Innovation Cycles

questions.question: Why does a General Purpose Technology like electricity deliver its economic benefits with a delay?
options: Because governments are slow to regulate new technologies
Because it requires reorganizing work, adapting infrastructure, and innovating at all levels of the value chain
Because consumers are inherently resistant to new technologies
Because GPTs are initially too expensive for widespread adoption
questions.explanation: GPTs require reorganizing systems, infrastructure, and processes before full benefits appear.
questions.category: General Purpose Technologies & Long Innovation Cycles

questions.question: Joseph Schumpeter's concept of "creative destruction" in the context of the digital economy means:
options: Digital technologies physically destroy old infrastructure
Innovation permanently disrupts existing economic structures, replacing old industries and jobs with new ones
Companies must destroy their existing products before launching new ones
Governments must deregulate industries to allow digital innovation
questions.explanation: Innovation permanently disrupts existing structures and replaces old industries and jobs with new ones.
questions.category: General Purpose Technologies & Long Innovation Cycles

questions.question: The "Productivity Paradox" in the information society refers to:
options: The fact that digital workers are more productive than manual workers
The observation that remarkable increases in computing power have not translated into proportionally fast productivity growth
The paradox that more data leads to less information
The contradiction between digital growth and environmental sustainability
questions.explanation: The Productivity Paradox refers to the gap between rapid technological progress and relatively slow measured productivity growth.
questions.category: Digital Economy — Forces, Paradoxes, and Sub-Economies

questions.question: Herbert Simon's concept of the "Attention Economy" is based on which fundamental insight?
options: Advertising revenue is the primary source of value in digital markets
Human attention is a scarce resource overwhelmed by the abundance of information
Artificial intelligence can replace human attention in decision-making
Social media platforms deliberately manipulate user attention for profit
questions.explanation: Simon argued that in an information-rich world, human attention becomes the scarce resource.
questions.category: Digital Economy — Forces, Paradoxes, and Sub-Economies

questions.question: According to the course, the digital economy can be understood as a convergence of several sub-economies. Which of the following is NOT listed as one of these sub-economies?
options: The Attention Economy
The Platform Economy
The Manufacturing Economy
The Sharing Economy
questions.explanation: The Manufacturing Economy is not listed; the course lists attention, knowledge, sharing, subscription, platform, and access economies.
questions.category: Digital Economy — Forces, Paradoxes, and Sub-Economies

questions.question: The "Access Economy" is characterized by:
options: Free access to all digital content and services
A preference for being given access to goods rather than owning them
Universal broadband internet access as a public utility
Open-source software replacing proprietary systems
questions.explanation: The Access Economy is defined by a shift from ownership to access.
questions.category: Digital Economy — Forces, Paradoxes, and Sub-Economies

questions.question: What is the "common element" that underlies all the sub-economies of the digital economy (Attention, Knowledge, Sharing, Subscription, Platform, Access)?
options: The dominance of American technology companies
The adoption of digital technologies
The replacement of physical goods with digital services
Government regulation of digital markets
questions.explanation: The common element across all these sub-economies is the adoption of digital technologies.
questions.category: Digital Economy — Forces, Paradoxes, and Sub-Economies

questions.question: The course states that "digitalization of all industries is rapidly blurring traditional sector borders." Which of the following best illustrates this phenomenon?
options: A bank opening more physical branches
A telecom company becoming a bank, or an industrial company becoming an IT company
A technology company hiring more engineers
A media company merging with another media company
questions.explanation: The course uses examples like a telecom company becoming a bank to show how digital transformation erases industry boundaries.
questions.category: Digital Economy — Forces, Paradoxes, and Sub-Economies

questions.question: According to the McKinsey Digital America Report (2015) referenced in the course, which sectors are BEST positioned to further digitize their activities?
options: Agricultural and extractive industries
Capital-intensive manufacturing sectors
Knowledge-intensive sectors such as ICT and media
Public sector and government services
questions.explanation: Knowledge-intensive sectors such as ICT and media are best placed to further digitize.
questions.category: Digital Economy — Forces, Paradoxes, and Sub-Economies

questions.question: According to the student notes, where is IoT currently positioned in the Technology Adoption Lifecycle?
options: Early Adopters
Early Majority
Late Majority
Innovators
questions.explanation: According to the student notes, IoT is in the Late Majority phase.

questions.question: According to the student notes, what is the PRIMARY barrier preventing IoT from reaching full market saturation (Laggards)?
options: Insufficient processing power in IoT devices
Lack of wireless connectivity standards
Trust, privacy concerns, and complexity of setup
High cost of semiconductor components
questions.explanation: The main barriers are trust, privacy concerns, and complexity of setup.

questions.question: The EU Cyber Resilience Act is mentioned in the student notes as relevant to IoT adoption. What role does it play?
options: It subsidizes IoT hardware for small businesses
It mandates IoT security standards, addressing privacy and security concerns
It establishes a universal IoT communication protocol
It regulates the data collected by IoT devices for commercial use
questions.explanation: The Cyber Resilience Act is cited as a step toward mandatory IoT security standards.

questions.question: According to the student notes, where is Blockchain currently positioned in the Technology Adoption Lifecycle, and what is the associated risk?
options: Late Majority, with risk of market saturation
Early Majority, with significant chasm risk
Early Adopters, with risk of never reaching mainstream
Laggards, with risk of complete obsolescence
questions.explanation: Blockchain is positioned in the Early Majority phase with significant chasm risk.

questions.question: What does the student notes identify as Blockchain's "identity crisis" that prevents it from reaching the Late Majority?
options: Uncertainty about whether it is a public or private technology
Being simultaneously a financial instrument, a database, a governance tool, and a social movement without a clear dominant use case
Confusion between Blockchain and cryptocurrency among regulators
Disagreement between developers about which programming language to use
questions.explanation: Blockchain's core problem is identity crisis — it lacks a clear dominant use case.

questions.question: The student notes mention a "WhatsApp moment" as what Blockchain needs. What does this metaphor mean?
options: Blockchain needs to be acquired by a major tech company like Meta
Blockchain needs one application so useful that users adopt it without caring about the underlying technology
Blockchain needs to achieve the same number of users as WhatsApp
Blockchain needs to focus exclusively on messaging applications
questions.explanation: Blockchain needs one killer application where users get value without understanding the underlying technology.

questions.question: According to the student notes, where is Big Data currently positioned in the Technology Adoption Lifecycle?
options: Early Majority
Late Majority, approaching Laggards
Early Adopters
Innovators
questions.explanation: Big Data is in Late Majority / Approaching Laggards.
questions.category: Big Data in the Adoption Lifecycle

questions.question: According to the student notes, what is the PRIMARY remaining challenge for Big Data reaching full market saturation?
options: Insufficient storage capacity and processing speed
Organizational culture and cost accessibility, not technology maturity
Lack of qualified data scientists globally
Absence of cloud computing infrastructure in developing countries
questions.explanation: The remaining challenge is organizational culture and cost accessibility, not technology.
questions.category: Big Data in the Adoption Lifecycle

questions.question: According to the student notes, what is the consistent cross-cutting insight across all four technologies (IoT, AI, Big Data, Blockchain)?
options: All four technologies require massive government subsidies to achieve mainstream adoption
Technology readiness is no longer the bottleneck — the real barriers are human: regulation, trust, culture, and simplicity
All four technologies will eventually be replaced by quantum computing
The speed of adoption depends primarily on the size of the technology company promoting it
questions.explanation: Across all four technologies, the real barriers are human: regulation, trust, culture, and simplicity.

questions.question: The concept of "invisible technology" is implied in the student notes as a key condition for reaching the Late Majority. What does this mean?
options: Technologies that operate without consuming electricity
Technologies that deliver value without requiring users to understand the underlying mechanisms
Technologies that are hidden from government regulation
Technologies that replace human workers without being noticed
questions.explanation: Invisible technology means users benefit without needing to understand how it works.

questions.question: In the Technology Adoption Lifecycle, what typically happens to companies that fail to cross "The Chasm"?
options: They become dominant in niche markets permanently
They are acquired by larger competitors
They fail to achieve mainstream adoption and often disappear or remain marginal
They automatically transition to the Late Majority phase
questions.explanation: Failing to cross the Chasm usually means failing to achieve mainstream adoption.

questions.question: Which of the following pairs correctly matches a "component technology" with its corresponding "architectural technology"?
options: Compilers → Internet browser
Routers → Internet browser
Magnetic tape → Audio cassette player/recorder
Antenna → Mobile phone
questions.explanation: The course explicitly lists magnetic tape as a component technology and audio cassette player/recorder as the corresponding architectural technology.

questions.question: The course describes the Internet's evolution as moving from "convergence" to "divergence." What does this mean?
options: The Internet first unified different media and is now splitting into specialized ecosystems
The Internet first served consumers and is now serving businesses
The Internet first operated in the USA and is now global
The Internet first used wired connections and is now wireless
questions.explanation: The Internet first unified different media and is now splitting into specialized ecosystems.
questions.category: Digital Economy — Convergence, Divergence, and Industry Transformation

questions.question: The course defines "Today's Internet" as a combination of which elements?
options: Hardware, software, and data centers
People, machines, companies, software, databases, and network traffic
Consumers, producers, and regulators
Servers, clients, and protocols
questions.explanation: The course explicitly defines Today's Internet as People + Companies + Machines + Software + Data + Network Traffic.
questions.category: Digital Economy — Convergence, Divergence, and Industry Transformation

questions.question: The course states that the Digital Economy has evolved from "self-contained, local machines" to what?
options: A purely virtual economy with no physical components
A hyperconnected system of interrelated heterogeneous entities governed by different and possibly conflicting logics
A single global network controlled by a few dominant technology companies
A fully automated economy where human labor is no longer needed
questions.explanation: The Digital Economy has evolved into a hyperconnected system of interrelated heterogeneous entities governed by different logics.
questions.category: Digital Economy — Convergence, Divergence, and Industry Transformation

questions.question: The course compares the "Old Economy" and the "New Economy." Which of the following correctly contrasts them?
options: Old Economy = asset light; New Economy = asset heavy
Old Economy = diminishing returns; New Economy = increasing returns
Old Economy = global; New Economy = local
Old Economy = data-driven; New Economy = resource-driven
questions.explanation: The Old Economy is diminishing returns, while the New Economy is increasing returns.
questions.category: Digital Economy — Convergence, Divergence, and Industry Transformation

questions.question: The course notes that the Digital Economy is "highly virtual but not so immaterial." What does this apparent contradiction mean?
options: Digital services are free but require expensive hardware to access
While digital products and services appear virtual, they rely on massive physical infrastructure
Virtual reality technologies are still dependent on physical controllers
Digital companies have virtual offices but employ real people
questions.explanation: The digital economy appears virtual but depends on enormous physical infrastructure.
questions.category: Digital Economy — Convergence, Divergence, and Industry Transformation

questions.question: The course uses the telecommunications industry as an illustration of technology adoption. Which of the following best describes the transformation that occurred?
options: Telecom companies simply upgraded their cables from copper to fiber
The industry transitioned from analog circuit switching to digital packet switching, transforming companies and eliminating jobs like switchboard operators
Telecom companies merged into a single global monopoly
The industry shifted from voice calls to video calls as the primary service
questions.explanation: The fundamental change was the move from analog circuit switching to digital packet switching.

questions.question: The course mentions that companies like Nokia, Siris, Cegetel, and LDCOM have "RIP" status. What concept does this illustrate?
options: The importance of patent protection in the digital economy
Schumpeter's creative destruction — companies that failed to adapt to technological transitions disappeared
The danger of government regulation for private companies
The superiority of American technology companies over European ones
questions.explanation: These companies illustrate Schumpeter's creative destruction.

questions.question: In the computer industry evolution shown in the course, which sequence correctly represents the dominant design progression?
options: PC → Mainframe → Smartphone → Cloud computing
Mainframe → PC → Smartphone → Cloud computing
Cloud computing → Smartphone → PC → Mainframe
Smartphone → PC → Mainframe → Cloud computing
questions.explanation: The correct sequence is Mainframe → PC → Smartphone → Cloud computing.

questions.question: According to the course, the Digital Economy creates a situation where "abundance of something creates scarcity in other areas." Which pair best illustrates this dynamic?
options: Abundance of hardware → scarcity of software
Abundance of information/data → scarcity of human attention
Abundance of digital companies → scarcity of physical companies
Abundance of internet users → scarcity of bandwidth
questions.explanation: The abundance of information creates scarcity of human attention.

questions.question: The course argues that "not all industries are equal" in the digital race. What is the key differentiating factor?
options: The geographic location of the industry's headquarters
The level of knowledge intensity — knowledge-intensive sectors are best positioned to digitalize
The age of the industry — older industries digitalize faster due to more experience
The size of the industry — larger industries have more resources to invest in digitalization
questions.explanation: Knowledge intensity is the key differentiating factor in digitalization success.

questions.question: The concept of "Cyber-Physical Systems" (mentioned as a consequence of Moore's Law) refers to:
options: Computer systems that simulate physical environments in virtual reality
Systems where the boundary between the analog/physical world and the digital world has disappeared through sensors and processors
Physical security systems controlled by cybersecurity software
Industrial robots that replace human physical labor
questions.explanation: Cyber-physical systems are where the analog and digital worlds have gradually disappeared through sensors and processors.

questions.question: The course identifies "network effects" as important for understanding two phenomena. Which pair correctly identifies these two phenomena?
options: Technology pricing and market regulation
Economic value generation in information-driven industries AND technology adoption influenced by social dynamics
Hardware performance and software compatibility
Government policy and corporate strategy
questions.explanation: Network effects help explain value generation in information-driven industries and technology adoption via social dynamics.

questions.question: The course presents the "Knowledge Economy" as one of the sub-economies of the digital economy. What is its defining characteristic?
options: Economies where patents and intellectual property are the primary assets
Performing in today's world requires mastering different perspectives on data, information, and knowledge
Economies where universities and research institutions drive GDP growth
The replacement of manual labor with knowledge workers
questions.explanation: The Knowledge Economy requires mastering different perspectives on data, information, and knowledge.

questions.question: The course discusses the "Subscription Economy" as one of the digital sub-economies. Which of the following best characterizes it?
options: Economies where consumers subscribe to political parties or civic organizations
Economies where consumers increasingly rely on recurrent purchase patterns rather than one-time transactions
Economies where businesses subscribe to government services
Economies where data subscriptions replace physical product ownership
questions.explanation: The Subscription Economy relies on recurrent purchase patterns.

questions.question: According to the course, what distinguishes the "5th technological wave" (Global Digital Economy) from previous waves?
options: It is the first wave driven by private sector investment rather than government funding
It started in a single industry and is now permeating the entire economy, with AI as its most important GPT
It is the first wave to create unemployment at a global scale
It is exclusively driven by American and Chinese technology companies
questions.explanation: The 5th wave started in ICT and is now permeating the entire economy, with AI as its most important GPT.

questions.question: The course mentions that "data, information, and knowledge are increasingly becoming essential ingredients of our modern economy." How does this relate to Shannon's and Ackoff's contributions?
options: Shannon proved data has no value without information; Ackoff proved information has no value without knowledge

Shannon formalized the relationship between signals and information; Ackoff showed that beyond a certain data threshold, information diminishes — together suggesting that quality matters more than quantity
Both Shannon and Ackoff argued that more data always leads to more knowledge
Shannon focused on hardware transmission; Ackoff focused on software processing — together they define the modern data pipeline
questions.explanation: Shannon and Ackoff together suggest that in the data-rich digital economy, quality matters more than quantity.

questions.question: The course describes the transition from "convergence" to "divergence" in today's internet. Which of the following correctly identifies the CURRENT divergent ecosystems?
options: Email, SMS, phone calls, and fax
Social networks, web navigation/content indexing, cloud computing, and IoT
Television, radio, newspapers, and magazines
Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, 4G, and 5G
questions.explanation: The current divergent ecosystems are social networks, web navigation/content indexing, cloud computing, and IoT.

questions.question: The course's final summary states that "the Digital Economy blurs the borders between traditional industrial sectors." Which of the following is the BEST conceptual explanation for why this happens?
options: Digital companies are legally allowed to operate in multiple sectors simultaneously
Digital technologies, especially GPTs like AI, are pervasive — they can be applied as inputs across all sectors, dissolving the technological distinctiveness that once separated industries
Globalization has made national industrial policies ineffective
Large technology companies have enough capital to acquire companies in any sector
questions.explanation: Digital technologies are pervasive GPTs, so they blur sector boundaries by being applied across all sectors.
